title: Google's Willow Qubits Win a Game No Classical Strategy Can Match
excerpt: Willow won the magic square game 98.3% of the time against an 88.9% classical ceiling, as Google Quantum AI measured quantum contextuality at scale in Science.
body:
• Google Quantum AI qubits on the Willow processor won the magic square game 98.30% of the time, beating the best possible classical ceiling of 88.89%, in research published on the cover of Science.
  • The team measured quantum contextuality at χ = 5.590 ± 0.008, past the classical limit of 4 and within 7% of the quantum maximum of 6.
  • The same physics outperformed constrained classical strategies in tasks spanning up to 105 qubits, and the tests doubled as a sensitive new benchmark that caught subtle hardware errors.
  • For readers: this is a hardware and physics result, not a commercial quantum computer — Google itself frames it as evidence about what gives quantum machines their edge.

Google's Willow quantum processor has won a coordination game that no classical strategy can win as often, in new research that Google Quantum AI says demonstrates one of quantum mechanics' strangest properties surviving at scale. In the paper, published in Science, the team's qubits won the magic square game 98.3% of the time, against a best possible classical score of 88.89%.

A game built on an impossible grid

The magic square game starts with a 3-by-3 grid that cannot exist. Each row must multiply to +1 and each column to -1, and simple counting shows the grid would need both an even and an odd number of -1 entries at once. Turned into a game, one player is handed a row and the other a column, without communicating. Any plan agreed in advance is effectively a pre-written grid, so it loses at least one round in nine.

On Willow, each player held two qubits sharing two entangled Bell pairs instead of a pre-written table. Google played all nine versions of the game 100,000 times apiece — 900,000 rounds in total — and the qubits lost roughly one round in sixty, winning 98.30% of them (0.9830 ± 0.0001). The reason, the researchers argue, is quantum contextuality: a measurement result is not fixed in advance, but takes shape alongside the other measurements made with it.

"Our qubits coordinated better than any pre-written table allows."

— Google Quantum AI, Research blog

Putting a number on it

The team then measured how contextual the machine is, using a Bell–Kochen–Specker inequality that bundles row and column products into a single score, χ. Any system whose outcomes are predetermined scores at most 4; quantum mechanics allows up to 6. Willow measured χ = 5.590 ± 0.008, which Google describes as comfortably past the classical bound and only 7% away from the quantum limit. Because the test is state-independent, the score describes the machine itself rather than a carefully chosen input.

Does it survive at scale?

Contextuality had previously been shown mainly in small systems of a few particles. Google extended the tests in two directions. In a multiplayer GHZ parity game, the team played with up to 71 players, one per qubit, and stayed above the classical bound throughout, while also verifying genuine entanglement across 45 qubits. Separately, the team ran a hidden-linear-function problem — a task where theory traces a quantum advantage back to contextuality — on grids of up to 105 qubits, with success probabilities above one-half.

Google is careful about what this does not show. As its announcement puts it, the work demonstrates that contextuality "survives at scale on our quantum processor" and outperforms constrained classical strategies — a bounded-resource comparison, not a claim that Willow beats the best classical computers at general tasks.

An unexpected dividend: a better ruler

Running tasks that demand many qubits agree simultaneously surfaced subtle coherent errors that conventional random-circuit benchmarks tend to average away. Google suggests contextuality can therefore serve as a hardware benchmark with a ceiling set by physics itself — χ = 6 and a perfect win rate — which it says is relevant to structured applications such as simulating molecules for chemistry and materials science.

What to watch next

The paper links contextuality to the "magic states" that error-corrected quantum computers need to run full algorithms. Whether the benchmark changes how processors are compared — and whether other hardware teams report the same score — is the next test of the claim.
